entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14657"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.18.9-Luke.18.14">Lu 18:9-14</reference>. Parable of the Pharisee and the Publican.</title> <div sID="gen28324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14657"/><hi type="bold">11-12. stood--</hi>as the Jews in prayer (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.25">Mr 11:25</reference>).<div eID="gen28324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God, &c.--</hi>To have been kept from gross iniquities was undoubtedly a just cause of thankfulness to God; but instead of the devoutly humble, admiring frame which this should inspire, the Pharisee arrogantly severs himself from the rest of mankind, as quite above them, and, with a contemptuous look at the poor publican, thanks God that he has not to stand afar off like him, to hang down his head like a bulrush and beat his breast like him. But these are only his moral excellencies. His religious merits complete his grounds for congratulation. Not confining himself to the one divinely prescribed annual fast (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.29">Le 16:29</reference>), he was not behind the most rigid, who fasted on the second and fifth days of every week [Lightfoot], and gave the tenth not only of what the law laid under tithing, but of "all his gains." Thus, besides doing all his duty, he did works of supererogation; while sins to confess and spiritual wants to be supplied he seems to have felt none. What a picture of the Pharisaic character and religion! <div eID="gen28325" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14659"/><div sID="gen28331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14659"/><hi type="bold">14. rather than the other--</hi>The meaning is, "and not the other"; for the Pharisee was not seeking justification, and felt no need of it. This great law of the Kingdom of God is, in the teaching of Christ, inscribed, as in letters of gold, over its entrance gate. And in how many different forms is it repeated (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.6">Psa 138:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.6">147:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">Lu 1:53</reference>). To be self-emptied, or, "poor in spirit," is the fundamental and indispensable preparation for the reception of the "grace which bringeth salvation": wherever this exists, the "mourning" for it which precedes "comfort" and the earnest "hungerings and thirstings after righteousness" which are rewarded by the "fulness" of it, will, as we see here, be surely found. Such, therefore, and such only, are the justified ones (<reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job 33:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.18">Psa 34:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Is 57:15</reference>). <div eID="gen28331" type="x-p"/>

And in how many different forms is it repeated ( Psa 138:6 ; 147:6 ; Lu 1:53 ). Such, therefore, and such only, are the justified ones ( Job 33:27 , 28 ; Psa 34:18 ; Is 57:15 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14660"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.18.15-Luke.18.17">Lu 18:15-17</reference>. Little Children Brought to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen28332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14660"/><hi type="bold">15. infants--</hi>showing that some, at least, of those called in Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.13">Mt 19:13</reference>) and Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.13">Mr 10:13</reference>) simply "little" or "young children," were literally "babes."<div eID="gen28332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">touch them--</hi>or, as more fully in Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.13">Mt 19:13</reference>), "put His hands on them and pray," or invoke a "blessing" on them (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.16">Mr 10:16</reference>), according to venerable custom (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.14">Ge 48:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen28333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rebuked them--</hi>Repeatedly the disciples thus interposed to save annoyance and interruption to their Master; but, as the result showed, always against the mind of Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.23">Mt 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.39">Lu 18:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.40">40</reference>). Here, it is plain from our Lord's reply, that they thought the intrusion a useless one, as infants were not capable of receiving anything from Him. His ministrations were for grown people. <div eID="gen28334" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: Lu 18:15-17 . Little Children Brought to Christ. 15. infants-- showing that some, at least, of those called in Matthew ( Mt 19:13 ) and Mark ( Mr 10:13 ) simply "little" or "young children," were literally "babes." touch them-- or, as more fully in Matthew ( Mt 19:13 ), "put His hands on them and pray," or invoke a "blessing" on them ( Mr 10:16 ), according to venerable custom ( Ge 48:14 , 15 ). rebuked them-- Repeatedly the disciples thus interposed to save annoyance and interruption to their Master; but, as the result showed, always against the mind of Christ ( Mt 15:23 ; Lu 18:39 , 40 ). Here, it is plain from our Lord's reply, that they thought the intrusion a useless one, as infants were not capable of receiving anything from Him. His ministrations were for grown people.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14661"/><div sID="gen28335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14661"/><hi type="bold">16. But Jesus--</hi>"much displeased," says Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.14">Mr 10:14</reference>); and invaluable addition.<div eID="gen28335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">said--</hi>"Suffer the little children to come unto Me"--"AND FORBID THEM NOT," is the important addition of Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.14">Mt 19:14</reference>) and Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.14">Mr 10:14</reference>). What words are these from the lips of Christ! The price of them is above rubies. But the reason assigned, "For of such is the Kingdom of God," or "of heaven," as in <reference osisRef="Matt.19.14">Mt 19:14</reference>, completes the previous information here conveyed; especially as interpreted by what immediately follows: "And He took them up in His arms, put His hands upon them, and blessed them" (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.16">Mr 10:16</reference>). It is surely not to be conceived that all our Lord meant was to inform us, that seeing grown people must become childlike in order to be capable of the Kingdom of God, therefore they should not hinder infants from coming to Him, and therefore He took up and blessed the infants themselves. Was it not just the grave mistake of the disciples that infants should not be brought to Christ, because only grown people could profit by Him, which "much displeased" our Lord? And though He took the irresistible opportunity of lowering their pride of reason, by informing them that, in order to enter the Kingdom, "instead of the children first becoming like them, they must themselves become like the children" [Richter in Stier], this was but by the way; and, returning to the children themselves, He took them up in His gracious arms, put His hands upon them and blessed them, for no conceivable reason but to show that they were thereby made capable, AS INFANTS, of the Kingdom of God. And if so, then "Can any man forbid water that these should not be baptized which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?" (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.47">Ac 10:47</reference>). But such application of the baptismal water can have no warrant here, save where the infants have been previously brought to Christ Himself for His benediction, and only as the sign and seal of that benediction.<div eID="gen28336" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.18.18-Luke.18.30">Lu 18:18-30</reference>. The Rich Young Ruler and Discourse Thereon.</title> <div sID="gen28337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This case presents some remarkable points. (1) The man was of irreproachable moral character; and this amidst all the temptations of youth, for he was a "young man" (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.22">Mt 19:22</reference>), and wealth, for "he was very rich" (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.23">Lu 18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.22">Mr 10:22</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2</reference>) But restless notwithstanding, his heart craves eternal life. (3) Unlike the "rulers," to whose class he belonged (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.18">Lu 18:18</reference>), he so far believed in Jesus as to be persuaded He could authoritatively direct him on this vital point. (4) So earnest is he that he comes "running" and even "kneeling before Him," and that when He was gone forth into the war (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.17">Mr 10:17</reference>)--</hi>the high-road, by this time crowded with travellers to the passover; undeterred by the virulent opposition of the class he belonged to as a "ruler" and by the shame he might be expected to feel at broaching such a question in the hearing of a crowd and on the open road. <div eID="gen28337" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14662"/><div sID="gen28338" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14662"/><hi type="bold">19. Why, &c.--</hi>Did our Lord mean then to teach that God only ought to be called "good?" Impossible, for that had been to contradict all Scripture teaching, and His own, too (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">Psa 112:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.21">Mt 25:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.8">Tit 1:8</reference>). Unless therefore we are to ascribe captiousness to our Lord, He could have had but one object--to raise the youth's ideas of Himself, as not to be classed merely with other "good masters," and declining to receive this title apart from the "One" who is essentially and only "good." This indeed is but distantly hinted; but unless this is seen in the background of our Lord's words, nothing worthy of Him can be made out of them. (Hence, Socinianism, instead of having any support here, is only baffled by it). <div eID="gen28338" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14663"/><div sID="gen28339" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14663"/><hi type="bold">20. Thou knowest, &c.--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.17">Mt 19:17</reference>) is more complete here: "but if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments. He saith unto him, Which--as if he had said, Point me out one of them which I have not kept?--"Jesus said, Thou shalt," &c. (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.17">Mt 19:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.19.18">18</reference>). Our Lord purposely confines Himself to the second table, which He would consider easy to keep, enumerating them all--for in Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.19">Mr 10:19</reference>), "Defraud not" stands for the tenth (else the eighth is twice repeated). In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.19">Mt 19:19</reference>) the sum of this second table of the law is added, "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself," as if to see if he would venture to say he had kept that. <div eID="gen28339" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 20. Thou knowest, &c.-- Matthew ( Mt 19:17 ) is more complete here: "but if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments. He saith unto him, Which--as if he had said, Point me out one of them which I have not kept?--"Jesus said, Thou shalt," &c. ( Mt 19:17 , 18 ). Our Lord purposely confines Himself to the second table, which He would consider easy to keep, enumerating them all--for in Mark ( Mr 10:19 ), "Defraud not" stands for the tenth (else the eighth is twice repeated). In Matthew ( Mt 19:19 ) the sum of this second table of the law is added, "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself," as if to see if he would venture to say he had kept that.

All these, &c.--</hi>"what lack I yet?" adds Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.20">Mt 19:20</reference>). Ah! <hi type="bold">this gives us a glimpse of his heart. Doubtless he was perfectly sincere; but something within whispered to him that his keeping of the commandments was too easy a way of getting to heaven. He felt something beyond this to be necessary; after keeping all the commandments he was at a loss to know what that could be; and he came to Jesus just upon that point. "Then," says Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.21">Mr 10:21</reference>), "Jesus beholding him loved him," or "looked lovingly upon him." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14665"/><div sID="gen28341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14665"/><hi type="bold">22. lackest ... one thing--</hi>Ah! but that a fundamental, fatal lack.<div eID="gen28341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sell, &c.--</hi>As riches were his idol, our Lord, who knew if from the first, lays His great authoritative grasp at once upon it, saying, "Now give Me up that, and all is right." No general direction about the disposal of riches, then, is here given, save that we are to sit loose to them and lay them at the feet of Him who gave them. He who does this with all he has, whether rich or poor, is a true heir of the kingdom of heaven. <div eID="gen28342" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14666"/><div sID="gen28343" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14666"/><hi type="bold">23-25. was very sorrowful--</hi>Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.22">Mt 19:22</reference>) more fully, "went away sorrowful"; Mark still more, "was sad" or "sullen" at that saying, and "went away grieved." Sorry he was, very sorry, to part with Christ; but to part with his riches would have cost him a pang more. When Riches or Heaven, on Christ's terms, were the alternative, the result showed to which side the balance inclined. Thus was he shown to lack the one all-comprehensive requirement of the law--the absolute subjection of the heart to God, and this want vitiated all his other obediences. <div eID="gen28343" type="x-p"/>

Blind Man Healed.</title> <div sID="gen28361" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Matt.20.29-Matt.20.34">Mt 20:29-34</reference>, they are two, as in the case of the Demoniac of Gadara. In Matthew and Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.46-Mark.10.52">Mr 10:46-52</reference>) the occurrence is connected with Christ's departure from Jericho; in Luke with His approach to it. Many ways of accounting for these slight divergences of detail have been proposed. Perhaps, if we knew all the facts, we should see no difficulty; but that we have been left so far in the dark shows that the thing is of no moment any way. One thing is plain, there could have been no collusion among the authors of these Gospels, else they would have taken care to remove these "spots on the sun." <div eID="gen28361" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14677"/><div sID="gen28365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14677"/><hi type="bold">40. commanded, &c.--</hi>Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.49">Mr 10:49</reference>) has this interesting addition: "And they call the blind man, saying unto him, Be of good comfort, rise, He calleth thee"--just as one earnestly desiring an interview with some exalted person, but told by one official after another that it is vain to wait, as he will not succeed (they know it), yet persists in waiting for some answer to his suit, and at length the door opens, and a servant appears, saying, "You will be admitted--he has called you." And are there no other suitors to Jesus who sometimes fare thus?
